newsitem.title: UK: Trade constraints may force further EU farm reform.
newsitem.headline: Trade constraints may force further EU farm reform.

text.p: International trade constraints rather than budget pressures are likely to force further reform of EU farm policy, said Dirk Ahner, head of the European Commission's agricultural policy unit.
Ahner was referring to EU commitments under the 1994 world farm trade agreement to reduce subsidised exports and open markets to more imports.
"If we stay with the current agriculture guideline I see less problem there than on the trade side," Ahner said on Tuesday in reply to a question at the Oxford Farming Conference.
The guideline he was referring to was the limit on farm spending growth originally agreed by ministers in 1988.
"Immediately I do not see any major budget constraints coming up," Ahner said.
His ideas contrast sharply with those of an earlier speaker at the conference, US agricultural economist Professor Abner Womack, whoe foresaw budget problems forcing change on the EU.
But a further switch to direct aid payments to farmers, rather than support through prices, could create problems over the cost of the EU's Common Agriculture Policy (CAP).
By making the level of spending more transparent, it could mean an increase in the level of opposition by taxpayers to the cost of the CAP.
Ahner added that there was a risk that EU stocks of the main agricultural products will pile up again, once the 10 planned new members in central and eastern Europe take their place.
"To be clear, we do not expect, as has been predicted, that there will be a rapid explosion of production and surpluses in the new countries," Ahner said.

"In fact there are still too many structural handicaps in the agricultural economies, but also in the upstream and downstream sectors linked to agriculture which these countries will have to overcome first," he said in a speech.
Ahner estimated the extra farm spending at 12 to 13 billion Ecus by the end of the first decade of the next century, if all ten candidates accede during that period.

The combination of the pressure from new members and likely extra limits on EU exports, as another round of world trade talks puts a new cap on export subsidies, would oblige the EU to impose an arable set-aside rate 25-26 per cent, according to Ahner's calculations.
There would also need to be cuts in dairy quotas and increased regulation in the beef sector.
"In all cases, our share in world trade would diminish sharply," he said.
"Is this the way we want to go?" The creation of more jobs and income sources outside agriculture was, therefore, a major challenge for rural development policy in Europe.
